summary.text:
A north Nottinghamshire district running a large, HRA-heavy balance sheet and quietly turning internal borrowing into external borrowing over five years. Total CFR is £180.5m in 2026/27, rising to £216.4m by 2030/31; 76% of that sits on the HRA in 2026/27 and 79% by 2030/31. External borrowing at 31 December 2025 was £95.163m (PWLB £71.363m, LOBOs £20.800m, LA short-term £3.000m); treasury investments were £30.815m. That leaves internal borrowing of £85.3m at end 2026/27 growing to £121.2m by 2030/31, and the paper's own p.9 quantifies the resulting cumulative borrowing requirement at £95.9m over five years — £66.6m for new capital plus £28m to refinance maturing loans.

The reconciliation ties honestly. Our file holds 14 PWLB loans for Bassetlaw totalling £68.363m at a weighted 3.9167%, within £3m of the paper's £71.363m PWLB figure at 31 December 2025 — the gap consistent with maturities in the intervening eight months (paper's Table 3.1 shows £15.5m maturing in 2026/27; our three shortest positions are £12.5m under 12 months at a weighted 3.643%). We hold no LOBOs and no LA temporary lending, so the £20.8m LOBO block and the £3.0m LA short-term line are the council's to see; ours is PWLB only.

Two features stand out. First, the HRA financing-cost ratio moves from 13% of HRA revenue in 2026/27 to 18% by 2029/30 as the HRA CFR grows from £136.3m to £170.2m and new borrowing is drawn at PWLB rates well above the average coupon on the existing book. The General Fund equivalent goes from -1% (net earning on treasury) to 3% as the cumulative borrowing lands. Second, the DMO's premature redemption curve at 14 August prices Bassetlaw's 14-loan book at an indicative net discount of £4.8m — 7.0% of principal, with 13 loans below par and only the £2m 2027 loan above. The paper's paragraph 3.6 says premature redemption rates remain elevated and any rescheduling depends on surplus cash; our engine agrees on direction, and the surplus-cash constraint is real given the under-borrowing.

The Council meeting is 26 February 2026 — six months in the past today. There is no next-meeting hook to write ahead of; the mid-year and outturn cadence implies further treasury items in autumn 2026 and early summer 2026 respectively, and neither is in our hold. Note is drafted; blocked on an officer address (this appendix names roles — Head of Finance and Property, Finance Manager — but no individuals, and no email addresses appear anywhere in the 33 pages).

officer.body:
Hi [NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 that went to Council on 26 February (item 5b, Appendix 1). You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The paper is clearly laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A reconciliation first, which came out clean. We hold 14 PWLB loans for Bassetlaw totalling £68.363m at a weighted 3.9167%, against the £71.363m PWLB in your Treasury Portfolio table on p.11 at 31 December 2025. The £3m gap is consistent with your Table 3.1 (p.12) — £15.5m of loans mature in 2026/27, and our three shortest positions (£12.5m under 12 months at a weighted 3.64%) fit that shape. We hold no LOBOs and no local-authority short-term positions, so the £20.8m LOBO block and the £3.0m LA borrowing line are yours to see; ours is PWLB only.

The line that carries most of the strategy is on p.12. Under-borrowing sits at £85.3m in 2026/27 and grows to £121.2m by 2030/31 as the CFR rises from £180.5m to £216.4m while external borrowing is held flat at £95.163m in the projection. Your own paragraph 2.6 (p.9) puts the cumulative borrowing requirement at £95.9m over five years — £66.6m of net financing need plus £28m to refinance maturing loans. Roughly three-quarters of the outer-year CFR is HRA: the HRA CFR moves from £136.3m to £170.2m while the General Fund holds close to £46m. On our fixing yesterday afternoon (PWLB notice 314/26 PM, 14 August) 10-year certainty is 5.83% and 25-year 6.46%; the HRA equivalent — standard less 60bp — is 40bp cheaper again, subject to the extension you flag on p.15 having been confirmed after January.

Your HRA financing-cost ratio moves from 13% of HRA revenue in 2026/27 to 18% by 2029/30 (p.7). The General Fund equivalent is negative in 2026/27 (-1%) and reaches 3% by 2030/31 as the cumulative borrowing lands — briefly net earning on treasury before the debt build catches up. It's an unusual shape for a district: two ratios moving in the same direction, driven by the same underlying £95.9m of new debt, but from very different starting points.

One more, on the redemption position. Your paragraph 3.6 (p.16) says premature redemption rates remain elevated and any rescheduling depends on surplus cash. On the DMO's premature redemption curve at yesterday's PM fixing (notice 314/26) our engine prices your 14-loan book at an indicative net discount of £4.8m — 7.0% of principal, with 13 of the 14 loans below par and only the £2m 2027 loan above. Break costs are indicative only; the DMO's quote is the only binding one, and we do not model MRP or accounting treatment. It's the size of the position on today's curve, not a recommendation on what to do with it.

Your daily-priced position is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. The sector context for what the PWLB is actually lending each month sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July's lending was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, so a thin month, and inter-authority money tends to firm up when PWLB activity thins.

On training, four fit. HRA treasury & self-financing speaks to three-quarters of your outer CFR. LOBO loans (legacy) covers the mechanics behind the £20.8m LOBO block; for context, we have logged eleven LOBO calls across councils we have read this year, all refused. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice picks up the £129.7m cumulative borrowing requirement your Section 2.5 quantifies. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator, given the current shape of the DMO curve. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
